proper-density-definition-3a1c0570.title: Proper Density Definition
proper-density-definition-3a1c0570.description: This equation defines the proper density (or rest density) of an object or system, which is its density measured in its own rest frame.
proper-density-definition-3a1c0570.conceptual_definition: Proper density, denoted by $\lambda_0$, is the density of a substance or system as measured by an observer who is at rest relative to the substance or system. It represents the intrinsic density unaffected by relativistic effects of motion. In the context of relativistic fluid dynamics or mass-energy density, it is the density observed in the frame where the bulk of the matter is stationary.
proper-density-definition-3a1c0570.interpretation: The equation $\lambda = \lambda_0$ signifies that the observed density $\lambda$ is equal to the proper density $\lambda_0$ when the observer is in the same inertial frame as the object or fluid. This occurs when the relative velocity between the observer and the object is zero, or negligibly small compared to the speed of light. It serves as the baseline density from which relativistic density changes are measured, as described by the full relativistic density formula $\lambda = \lambda_0 \gamma$.
proper-density-definition-3a1c0570.limits_and_boundary: This equation is valid specifically in the proper frame of reference of the object or system, where its velocity relative to the observer is zero. It also holds true in the non-relativistic limit where the Lorentz factor $\gamma$ approaches 1, meaning velocities are much smaller than the speed of light (v \ll c).
proper-density-definition-3a1c0570.symmetry_origin: This equation itself is a definition of density in a specific reference frame (the proper frame). While not directly a symmetry, the concept of proper density is an invariant scalar under Lorentz transformations when considered as the rest mass density. It is the fundamental quantity that transforms under Lorentz boosts, leading to the relativistic density formula.

semantic_variables.\\lambda: Observed density of the object or system, as measured by an arbitrary observer (SI unit: kg/m³).
semantic_variables.\\lambda_0: Proper density (or rest density) of the object or system, measured in its own rest frame (SI unit: kg/m³).

gravitational-geodesic-acceleration-term.title: Gravitational Geodesic Acceleration Term
gravitational-geodesic-acceleration-term.description: This term represents the acceleration experienced by a particle due to the curvature of spacetime, as described by the Christoffel symbols and the particle's four-velocity.
gravitational-geodesic-acceleration-term.conceptual_definition: In general relativity, particles in free fall follow geodesics, which are the 'straightest possible' paths in curved spacetime. The Christoffel symbols, \Gamma^$\mu$_{$\alpha$\beta$}, quantify how spacetime is curved, effectively replacing the concept of a gravitational force. This term describes the rate of change of the four-velocity components due to this curvature, representing the gravitational contribution to the four-acceleration.
gravitational-geodesic-acceleration-term.interpretation: This term dictates how the four-velocity of a particle changes solely due to the presence of a gravitational field (i.e., curved spacetime). It is the non-force component of acceleration in general relativity, meaning it describes the 'inertial' motion along a geodesic. A particle experiencing only gravity will have its four-acceleration entirely determined by this term (in the absence of non-gravitational forces). The negative sign indicates that it acts to change the direction of motion in a way that corresponds to attraction in Newtonian gravity.
gravitational-geodesic-acceleration-term.limits_and_boundary: In flat spacetime (Minkowski spacetime), all Christoffel symbols \Gamma^$\mu$_{$\alpha$\beta$} are zero, and this term vanishes, implying no gravitational acceleration. In the weak-field limit and for slow speeds, this term reduces to the Newtonian gravitational acceleration. It applies to both massive and massless particles, though for massless particles, the four-velocity is a null vector.
gravitational-geodesic-acceleration-term.symmetry_origin: This term arises directly from the principle of general covariance, which states that the laws of physics should take the same form in all coordinate systems. It is a consequence of the equivalence principle, which equates gravitational and inertial mass, and the idea that gravity is a manifestation of spacetime curvature. It is also linked to local Lorentz invariance.

semantic_variables.\\Gamma^\\mu_{\\alpha\\beta}: Christoffel symbols of the second kind. Units: per meter (m^-1). These are the connection coefficients that describe how basis vectors change in curved spacetime, encoding the gravitational field.
semantic_variables.U^\\alpha: Contravariant component of the four-velocity vector. Units: meters per second (m/s). Represents the rate of change of a particle's spacetime position with respect to proper time.
semantic_variables.U^\\beta: Contravariant component of the four-velocity vector. Units: meters per second (m/s). Represents the rate of change of a particle's spacetime position with respect to proper time.

parallel-component-of-acceleration-7d4ca.title: Parallel Component of Acceleration
parallel-component-of-acceleration-7d4ca.description: This vector represents the component of the total acceleration vector that is parallel to the instantaneous velocity vector.
parallel-component-of-acceleration-7d4ca.conceptual_definition: The parallel component of acceleration, $\mathbf{a}$_\parallel, is responsible for changing the magnitude (speed) of an object's velocity. It acts along the direction of motion, either increasing or decreasing the speed. It is one of two orthogonal components into which the total acceleration vector can be decomposed, the other being the perpendicular component.
parallel-component-of-acceleration-7d4ca.interpretation: Physically, $\mathbf{a}$_\parallel quantifies how quickly an object's speed is changing. If $\mathbf{a}$_\parallel is in the same direction as $\mathbf{v}$, the object is speeding up; if it's in the opposite direction, the object is slowing down. In curvilinear motion, it describes the tangential acceleration. Its magnitude is given by the rate of change of speed, d|$\mathbf{v}$|/dt.
parallel-component-of-acceleration-7d4ca.limits_and_boundary: If the velocity vector $\mathbf{v}$ is zero, the parallel component is undefined in its standard projection form, as the direction of motion is not established. If the total acceleration $\mathbf{a}$ is purely perpendicular to $\mathbf{v}$ (e.g., uniform circular motion), then $\mathbf{a}$_\parallel = 0. If $\mathbf{a}$ is purely parallel to $\mathbf{v}$ (e.g., linear motion), then $\mathbf{a}$_\parallel = $\mathbf{a}$.
parallel-component-of-acceleration-7d4ca.symmetry_origin: The decomposition of acceleration into parallel and perpendicular components arises from the fundamental properties of vector spaces and the ability to project one vector onto another. This decomposition is invariant under rotations of the coordinate system, provided the relative orientation of acceleration and velocity vectors is preserved.

semantic_variables.\\mathbf{a}_\\parallel: The parallel component of the acceleration vector, measured in meters per second squared (m/s\textasciicircum2). It is defined as \frac{(\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{v})}{|\mathbf{v}|^2} \mathbf{v}.
semantic_variables.\\mathbf{a}: The total acceleration vector of the particle, measured in meters per second squared (m/s\textasciicircum2).
semantic_variables.\\mathbf{v}: The instantaneous velocity vector of the particle, measured in meters per second (m/s).
semantic_variables.\\cdot: The dot product (scalar product) operator, which yields a scalar value from two vectors.
semantic_variables.|\\mathbf{v}|^2: The square of the magnitude (speed) of the velocity vector, measured in meters squared per second squared (m\textasciicircum2/s\textasciicircum2).

critical-density-formula-8d1d04be.title: Critical Density Formula
critical-density-formula-8d1d04be.description: This formula defines the critical density of the universe, a key cosmological parameter that determines the universe's spatial geometry. It relates the Hubble parameter to fundamental constants.
critical-density-formula-8d1d04be.conceptual_definition: The critical density, denoted $\rho_c$, is the specific total energy density required for the universe to be spatially flat, meaning its expansion rate would asymptotically approach zero over infinite time without recollapsing. It is derived from the Friedmann equations, which are the cornerstone of modern cosmology, describing the dynamics of a homogeneous and isotropic universe. This density serves as a crucial benchmark for classifying the universe's overall curvature.
critical-density-formula-8d1d04be.interpretation: The value of $\rho_c$ is not constant but evolves with the Hubble parameter, H, as the universe expands. At any given cosmic epoch, it represents the dividing line: if the actual average energy density of the universe ($\rho$) is greater than $\rho_c$, the universe is spatially closed; if $\rho$ < $\rho_c$, it is spatially open; and if $\rho$ = $\rho_c$, it is spatially flat. This concept is fundamental to defining the density parameter \Omega = $\rho$ / $\rho_c$, which is a direct measure of the universe's curvature.
critical-density-formula-8d1d04be.limits_and_boundary: This formula is applicable within the framework of general relativity and the cosmological principle, assuming a large-scale homogeneous and isotropic universe (FLRW metric). It is valid for any epoch where the Hubble parameter H is defined. The formula does not account for local inhomogeneities but describes the average density required for global flatness.
critical-density-formula-8d1d04be.symmetry_origin: The derivation of the critical density formula is rooted in the cosmological principle, which postulates that the universe is homogeneous and isotropic on sufficiently large scales. These symmetries simplify Einstein's field equations to the Friedmann equations, from which the expression for $\rho_c$ is directly obtained.

semantic_variables.\\rho_c: Critical density of the universe (kg/m^3). The total energy density required for a spatially flat universe, defined as \rho_c = \frac{3H^2}{8\pi G}.
semantic_variables.H: Hubble parameter (s^-1). Represents the expansion rate of the universe at a given cosmic time.
semantic_variables.G: Newton's gravitational constant (N m^2 kg^-2). A fundamental physical constant quantifying the strength of gravitational attraction.

sum-of-transverse-momenta-magnitudes-b40.title: Sum of Transverse Momenta Magnitudes
sum-of-transverse-momenta-magnitudes-b40.description: This equation represents the scalar sum of the magnitudes of the transverse momenta of all reconstructed particles within a given event. It quantifies the total "transverse activity" in a particle collision.
sum-of-transverse-momenta-magnitudes-b40.conceptual_definition: In high-energy collider experiments, particles are produced with momentum components both along (longitudinal) and perpendicular (transverse) to the beam axis. The transverse momentum, p_T, is the component of momentum perpendicular to the beam direction. The sum of the magnitudes of these transverse momenta, \sum |p_T|, serves as a robust observable to characterize the overall energy scale and complexity of an event, particularly in searches for new, heavy particles.
sum-of-transverse-momenta-magnitudes-b40.interpretation: This quantity is a scalar measure of the total momentum imbalance in the plane perpendicular to the colliding beams. Unlike the vector sum of transverse momenta (which should ideally be zero due to momentum conservation), the scalar sum \sum |p_T| provides an indication of how much momentum was carried by *all* detected particles in the transverse plane, regardless of their direction. It is a key variable in event selection and background rejection in particle physics analyses, often used in conjunction with missing transverse energy to identify events with invisible particles.
sum-of-transverse-momenta-magnitudes-b40.limits_and_boundary: The value of \sum |p_T| is always non-negative, as it is a sum of magnitudes. Its minimum value is zero, which would occur in an idealized event where all particles are produced perfectly collinear with the beam axis. There is no theoretical upper bound, as it scales with the energy of the collision and the multiplicity of particles produced.
sum-of-transverse-momenta-magnitudes-b40.symmetry_origin: While \sum |p_T| itself is not a conserved quantity, its utility arises from the conservation of momentum in the transverse plane. The individual transverse momenta are defined relative to the beam axis, which is a direction of approximate cylindrical symmetry in collider experiments. The sum is invariant under rotations around the beam axis.

semantic_variables.p_T: Transverse momentum of a particle (kg\cdot m/s). This is the component of a particle's momentum perpendicular to the beam axis in a collider experiment.
semantic_variables.|p_T|: Magnitude of the transverse momentum of a particle (kg\cdot m/s). This represents the scalar value of the momentum component perpendicular to the beam axis.
semantic_variables.\\sum: Summation operator, indicating the sum over all relevant particles in an event.

infinitesimal-displacement-in-theta-dire.title: Infinitesimal Displacement in Theta Direction
infinitesimal-displacement-in-theta-dire.description: Represents the infinitesimal arc length element along the polar angle \(\theta\) in spherical coordinates, given by the formula \(ds_\theta = r \, d\theta\).
infinitesimal-displacement-in-theta-dire.conceptual_definition: In spherical coordinates, an infinitesimal displacement vector can be decomposed into orthogonal components along the radial, polar, and azimuthal directions. This specific component, $ds_\theta = r \, d\theta$, quantifies the small change in position resulting from an infinitesimal change in the polar angle $\theta$ while keeping the radial distance $r$ and azimuthal angle $\phi$ constant. It is essentially an arc length element on a sphere of radius $r$ for a given change in $\theta$.
infinitesimal-displacement-in-theta-dire.interpretation: The term $ds_\theta$ signifies the physical distance covered when the polar angle $\theta$ changes by an infinitesimal amount $d\theta$. Its magnitude is directly proportional to the radial distance $r$ from the origin, meaning that for a given $d\theta$, the actual physical displacement is larger further away from the origin. This component is fundamental for calculating line integrals, surface integrals, and volume integrals in spherical coordinate systems, particularly when analyzing physical phenomena that exhibit spherical symmetry.
infinitesimal-displacement-in-theta-dire.limits_and_boundary: The polar angle $\theta$ typically ranges from $0$ to $\pi$ radians. At $r=0$, $ds_\theta = 0$, indicating that at the origin, there is no displacement associated with a change in angle. For a fixed infinitesimal $d\theta$, $ds_\theta$ approaches infinity as $r$ approaches infinity, reflecting the increasing circumference of larger spheres.
infinitesimal-displacement-in-theta-dire.symmetry_origin: This formula arises from the geometric definition of arc length on a circle of radius $r$. It inherently reflects the rotational symmetry about the z-axis (azimuthal symmetry) and the spherical symmetry of the coordinate system itself, as it describes displacement on a spherical surface.

semantic_variables.ds_\\theta: Infinitesimal displacement along the polar angle \(\theta\) direction (meters)
semantic_variables.d\\theta: Infinitesimal change in the polar angle \(\theta\) (radians)

condition-for-non-spontaneous-process-9e.title: Condition for Non-Spontaneous Process
condition-for-non-spontaneous-process-9e.description: This condition defines when a thermodynamic process will not occur spontaneously under constant temperature and pressure.
condition-for-non-spontaneous-process-9e.conceptual_definition: For a process occurring at constant temperature and pressure, a positive change in Gibbs free energy (\Delta G > 0) indicates that the process is non-spontaneous. This means the system requires an input of energy from its surroundings to proceed, as it moves towards a higher free energy state.
condition-for-non-spontaneous-process-9e.interpretation: When the Gibbs free energy of a system increases during a process (\Delta G > 0), the process is thermodynamically unfavorable and will not proceed on its own. This implies that the reverse process would be spontaneous, or that external work must be supplied to drive the forward process. This criterion is a direct consequence of the second law of thermodynamics applied to systems at constant temperature and pressure.
condition-for-non-spontaneous-process-9e.limits_and_boundary: This criterion is strictly applicable for processes occurring at constant temperature and pressure. For processes at constant temperature and volume, the Helmholtz free energy (\Delta A) is used. For isolated systems, the total entropy change (\Delta S_{universe}) is the criterion.
condition-for-non-spontaneous-process-9e.symmetry_origin: Rooted in the Second Law of Thermodynamics, which dictates the direction of spontaneous change in the universe. Gibbs free energy provides a convenient state function to apply this law under specific constant conditions.

semantic_variables.\\Delta G: Change in Gibbs Free Energy (Joules, J). A positive value signifies that the process is non-spontaneous under constant temperature and pressure.

derivative-transformation-rotating-frame.title: Derivative Transformation (Rotating Frame)
derivative-transformation-rotating-frame.description: This equation relates the time derivative of a vector quantity as observed in an inertial frame to its time derivative as observed in a rotating frame, accounting for the frame's angular velocity.
derivative-transformation-rotating-frame.conceptual_definition: This formula is fundamental for analyzing motion in non-inertial (specifically, rotating) reference frames. It establishes the mathematical relationship between the rate of change of any vector quantity as observed from an inertial frame and as observed from a frame that is rotating with respect to the inertial frame. The cross product term explicitly accounts for the apparent change in direction of the vector due to the rotation of the coordinate system itself.
derivative-transformation-rotating-frame.interpretation: The equation $(d/dt)_{inertial} = (d/dt)_{rotating} + \mathbf{\omega} \times$ describes how the time derivative of any vector quantity (e.g., position, velocity, momentum) observed in an inertial frame relates to its time derivative observed in a frame rotating with angular velocity $\mathbf{\omega}$. The first term on the right, $(d/dt)_{rotating}$, represents the rate of change of the vector as measured by an observer fixed in the rotating frame. The second term, $\mathbf{\omega} \times$, is the 'transport term' or 'apparent' term, which arises because the basis vectors of the rotating frame are themselves changing direction with respect to the inertial frame. This term is crucial for understanding fictitious forces like the Coriolis and centrifugal forces, which appear when applying Newton's laws in rotating frames.
derivative-transformation-rotating-frame.limits_and_boundary: This equation is valid for any vector quantity. If the rotating frame is not rotating (i.e., $\mathbf{\omega} = 0$), then the equation reduces to $(d/dt)_{inertial} = (d/dt)_{rotating}$, as expected for two frames that are not rotating relative to each other. It assumes a constant angular velocity $\mathbf{\omega}$ for simplicity in its most common form, though it can be generalized for time-varying $\mathbf{\omega}$.
derivative-transformation-rotating-frame.symmetry_origin: This formula is a kinematic transformation derived from the principles of vector calculus and the definition of angular velocity. While not directly stemming from a symmetry or conservation law, it is consistent with the rotational symmetry of space, which implies that the laws of physics are invariant under rotations, provided transformations like this are applied to relate observations in different frames.

semantic_variables.(d/dt)_{inertial}: The time derivative of a vector quantity as measured by an observer in an inertial (non-accelerating) reference frame. Its units depend on the specific vector being differentiated (e.g., m/s for position, m/s^2 for velocity).
semantic_variables.(d/dt)_{rotating}: The time derivative of the same vector quantity as measured by an observer fixed in the rotating reference frame. Its units depend on the specific vector being differentiated.
semantic_variables.\\mathbf{\\omega}: The angular velocity vector of the rotating reference frame with respect to the inertial frame, measured in radians per second (rad/s). Its direction is along the axis of rotation, determined by the right-hand rule.
semantic_variables.\\times: The vector cross product operator, which yields a vector perpendicular to both input vectors, with magnitude equal to the product of their magnitudes and the sine of the angle between them.

positive-laplacian-of-scalar-potential-3.title: Positive Laplacian of Scalar Potential
positive-laplacian-of-scalar-potential-3.description: This inequality indicates a region where a scalar field, such as an electrostatic potential, is locally convex or has a local minimum, implying a net 'outward' flux of its gradient.
positive-laplacian-of-scalar-potential-3.conceptual_definition:
The Laplacian operator, 
abla^2, represents the divergence of the gradient of a scalar field. When 
abla^2 \Phi > 0, it signifies that the scalar field \Phi is locally convex at that point, meaning its value at that point is less than the average of its values in an infinitesimal neighborhood around it. In the context of potential fields, this implies a region where the field's 'curvature' is positive.
positive-laplacian-of-scalar-potential-3.interpretation:
In electrostatics, if \Phi is the electric potential, then 
abla^2 \Phi > 0 suggests a region where the potential has a local minimum. According to Poisson's equation ( 
abla^2 \Phi = -$\rho$ / \varepsilon_0), this would correspond to a region where the charge density $\rho$ is negative. Therefore, this inequality describes a spatial region where the electric potential behaves as if there is a net negative charge density, causing the potential to 'dip' locally. It signifies a point where the electric field lines are converging towards the point if it were a minimum.
positive-laplacian-of-scalar-potential-3.limits_and_boundary:
This inequality describes a local condition within a field rather than defining boundary conditions. It characterizes regions where the field exhibits a specific positive curvature. For instance, in a charge-free region, where Laplace's equation ( 
abla^2 \Phi = 0) holds, this inequality cannot be satisfied, implying its relevance only in regions with non-zero sources or sinks.
positive-laplacian-of-scalar-potential-3.symmetry_origin:
The Laplacian operator 
abla^2 is invariant under rotations and translations of the coordinate system, reflecting the isotropic and homogeneous nature of space in many physical contexts. This symmetry is inherited by the inequality.

semantic_variables.\\Phi: The scalar potential field, often representing electric potential in volts (V) in electrostatics, or gravitational potential in joules per kilogram (J/kg) in gravitation. It describes the potential energy per unit charge or mass at a given point in space.

quantum-lagrangian-time-derivative-term-.title: Quantum Lagrangian Time Derivative Term
quantum-lagrangian-time-derivative-term-.description: This term represents a component of the kinetic energy density within the Lagrangian formulation of quantum mechanics, specifically involving the time evolution of the quantum state.
quantum-lagrangian-time-derivative-term-.conceptual_definition: In quantum mechanics, this term, $i\hbar \psi^* \dot{\psi}$, is a crucial component of the Lagrangian density for a non-relativistic particle. It captures the time-dependent evolution of the quantum state, contributing to the kinetic energy part of the system's action. Its presence ensures the correct dynamics described by the Schrödinger equation when varied.
quantum-lagrangian-time-derivative-term-.interpretation: This term, when integrated over space and time, contributes to the action, whose variation with respect to the wavefunction yields the time-dependent Schrödinger equation. It is intrinsically linked to the concept of probability current density, describing the flow of probability in quantum systems. Its imaginary nature highlights its role in the phase evolution of the wavefunction rather than a direct observable energy.
quantum-lagrangian-time-derivative-term-.limits_and_boundary: This term is applicable within the framework of non-relativistic quantum mechanics. It assumes the wavefunction $\psi$ is sufficiently smooth and differentiable with respect to time, and that it satisfies appropriate boundary conditions for the physical system under consideration (e.g., vanishing at infinity for unbound states, or periodic/Dirichlet conditions for confined systems).
quantum-lagrangian-time-derivative-term-.symmetry_origin: This term is fundamental to the time evolution of quantum systems and is intrinsically linked to time translation symmetry. In the context of the full Lagrangian, this symmetry, via Noether's theorem, leads to the conservation of energy.

semantic_variables.i: The imaginary unit, defined as $\sqrt{-1}$. It is a dimensionless constant.
semantic_variables.\\hbar: Reduced Planck constant (Dirac constant), a fundamental physical constant representing the quantum of action. Its SI unit is Joule-second (J\cdot s).
semantic_variables.\\psi: The complex-valued wavefunction of the quantum system. In position space, its squared modulus, $|\psi|^2$, represents the probability density of finding the particle at a given position. Its SI unit depends on the dimensionality and normalization, typically m$^{-3/2}$ for a 3D system.
semantic_variables.\\psi^*: The complex conjugate of the wavefunction $\psi$. Its SI unit is the same as that of $\psi$, typically m$^{-3/2}$ for a 3D system.
semantic_variables.\\dot{\\psi}: The partial time derivative of the wavefunction $\psi$, representing its rate of change with respect to time. Its SI unit is the unit of $\psi$ per second, typically m$^{-3/2}\cdot s^{-1}$ for a 3D system.

relativistic-four-force-definition-f02b6.title: Relativistic Four-Force Definition
relativistic-four-force-definition-f02b6.description: This equation defines the relativistic four-force as the proper mass times the proper time derivative of the four-velocity.
relativistic-four-force-definition-f02b6.conceptual_definition: In special relativity, the four-force is a four-vector that generalizes the classical force vector, describing how the four-momentum of a particle changes with respect to its proper time. It is directly analogous to Newton's second law, $\mathbf{F}$ = m $\mathbf{a}$, but extended to spacetime. This formulation ensures that the equation is Lorentz covariant, meaning it holds true in all inertial reference frames.
relativistic-four-force-definition-f02b6.interpretation: This formula is a fundamental expression of relativistic dynamics, linking the cause of motion (4-force) to the change in the state of motion (4-velocity) for a particle with invariant proper mass. It shows that a four-force acting on a particle causes its four-velocity to change, with the proper mass acting as the inertial resistance to this change. The use of proper time \tau ensures that the rate of change is measured in a frame-independent manner, making the equation intrinsically relativistic and consistent with the master formula's implication of proper mass conservation.
relativistic-four-force-definition-f02b6.limits_and_boundary: This equation is valid for particles with constant proper mass m. It applies in flat spacetime (Minkowski spacetime) and can be generalized to curved spacetime by replacing the derivative with a covariant derivative. It is not directly applicable to systems where mass is not conserved or where the particle's internal structure changes significantly. For speeds much less than the speed of light, it reduces to the classical Newton's second law.
relativistic-four-force-definition-f02b6.symmetry_origin: This equation is a direct consequence of the Lorentz symmetry of spacetime, which dictates that the laws of physics must be the same in all inertial reference frames. It arises from the conservation of four-momentum and the definition of four-force as the proper time derivative of four-momentum, f^$\mu = \frac{dP^\mu}{d\tau}$, where P^$\mu$= mU^$\mu$. The orthogonality condition f^$\mu $U_$\mu$ = 0, which implies proper mass conservation, is a direct consequence of this definition and the constant magnitude of the four-velocity.

semantic_variables.f^\\mu: Four-force (or 4-force), a four-vector representing the relativistic generalization of force, measured in Newtons (N).
semantic_variables.m: Proper mass (or rest mass) of the particle, an invariant scalar quantity representing the mass of the particle in its rest frame, measured in kilograms (kg).
semantic_variables.U^\\mu: Four-velocity (or 4-velocity), a four-vector representing the relativistic generalization of velocity, defined as the proper time derivative of the four-position, measured in meters per second (m/s).
semantic_variables.\\tau: Proper time, the time measured by a clock moving with the particle, an invariant scalar quantity, measured in seconds (s).
